paragraphs: Predicting how a scene will change is especially difficult when it contains fluids or granular materials whose individual particles are hard to track. This paper introduces a system that learns physical dynamics from visual observations while representing the scene explicitly in three dimensions. Its goal is to support predictions without requiring detailed particle trajectories from a simulator.

The system combines a conditional Neural Radiance Field-style visual component with a dynamics predictor built around 3D points. This structure lets the model incorporate assumptions about spatial organization and relationships between scene elements. Training uses images from multiple viewpoints and imperfect object-instance masks obtained through color information. Those inputs replace the dense point-trajectory supervision used by earlier point-based approaches.

The authors generate simulated datasets involving fluids, granular materials, and rigid objects, without supplying dense particle information. In these settings, their model predicts far into the future and substantially outperforms models without explicit 3D representations. They also report strong generalization in tested extrapolation settings, supporting the value of a structured 3D representation when learning dynamics from images.
neurips-2023-3d-intphys-towards-more-gen.tldr: 3D-IntPhys learns to predict complex physical scenes from multiview images using an explicit 3D representation without dense particle supervision.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction compresses complex data into a smaller representation while trying to retain meaningful relationships. For data organized along a curved manifold, distances along that manifold can matter more than direct distances through the surrounding space. Diffusion-based methods were thought to preserve this geometry, but the abstract identifies a missing theoretical connection between their diffusion calculations and manifold distances.

The paper supplies that connection using results from Riemannian geometry that relate heat diffusion to distance. It also introduces heat geodesic embeddings, a more general embedding method based on heat kernels. This perspective makes the choices involved in representing and denoising data more explicit, grounding the embedding procedure in a relationship between how heat spreads and the geometry it spreads across.

Reported results show improved preservation of known manifold distances and cluster structure in toy datasets. On single-cell RNA-sequencing data containing both continuous variation and clusters, the method supports interpolation of withheld timepoints. Different parameter choices also produce results resembling PHATE and SNE, connecting these established approaches within the broader proposed framework.
neurips-2023-a-heat-diffusion-perspectiv.tldr: Heat geodesic embeddings connect diffusion to manifold distances and improve geometric preservation in the reported dimensionality-reduction experiments.

paragraphs: Brain-machine interfaces need to translate neural activity into useful movements in real time. This paper evaluates recurrent neural networks in closed-loop finger-control tasks, where decoding operates as part of ongoing control. The experiments use intracortical recordings from nonhuman primates and compare recurrent models with convolutional and transformer-based neural networks.

Across online tasks involving one or two fingers, LSTMs outperform the other tested architectures, averaging 18% higher throughput than the convolutional network. The authors also investigate how much a decoder can benefit from memorizing movement patterns. When tasks contain a reduced set of movements, recurrent decoders match able-bodied control. Performance declines as the movement set expands, but remains at least as high as fully continuous decoding.

A further experiment addresses a two-finger task in which one movement dimension has poor neural inputs. Training an RNN to combine movement classification with continuous decoding recovers functional control. Together, these findings suggest that learning reusable movement patterns can help real-time BMI performance, with the usefulness of memorization depending on the range of movements required.
neurips-2023-balancing-memorization-and-.tldr: Recurrent decoders improve real-time finger control in primate BMI experiments by combining continuous decoding with learned movement patterns.

paragraphs: Long sequences create a tension between modeling distant relationships and keeping computation manageable. State space models scale efficiently and have performed strongly in vision and audio, but the abstract notes that they still trail Transformers in language modeling. This paper proposes a hybrid layer that assigns different parts of sequence modeling to these two approaches.

The Block-State Transformer uses a state space sublayer to provide long-range context and a blockwise Transformer sublayer to represent shorter-range relationships. The authors study three fully parallelizable ways to integrate these components. The central idea is to combine the long-sequence efficiency of state space processing with attention operating within blocks, rather than asking either component to handle every scale of context alone.

The reported models achieve better language-modeling perplexity than similar Transformer-based architectures and generalize to longer sequences. With model parallelization, the proposed layer also runs more than ten times faster than the Block-Recurrent Transformer layer. That speed comparison concerns layer-level execution under parallelization, while the perplexity findings support the hybrid architecture's usefulness for language modeling.
neurips-2023-block-state-transformers-86.tldr: Block-State Transformers combine state space models with blockwise attention to improve reported language-modeling performance and parallelized layer speed.

paragraphs: A deployed model may encounter unfamiliar categories or inputs altered by adversarial perturbations. This paper explores detecting both kinds of unusual input through self-supervised contrastive learning. Its approach does not require labels for the ordinary training samples or examples of the out-of-distribution inputs it will later try to identify.

The authors first combine contrastive representations with the maximum mean discrepancy two-sample test. This tests whether two independent collections of observations come from the same distribution. They report distinguishing CIFAR-10 from CIFAR-10.1 with higher confidence than previous work. Building on this result, they introduce CADet for detecting anomalies one sample at a time, using similarities between contrastive transformations of that sample.

CADet outperforms existing adversarial-detection methods on adversarially perturbed ImageNet samples. For unfamiliar categories, it performs comparably to unseen-label detection methods on ImageNet-O and iNaturalist. These results support using contrastive representations for both group-level distribution testing and individual anomaly detection, while keeping the different reported outcomes clear: improved adversarial detection and comparable unseen-category detection.
neurips-2023-cadet-fully-self-supervised.tldr: CADet uses self-supervised contrastive similarities to detect unfamiliar and adversarial inputs without labeled training data or OOD examples.

paragraphs: Learning to make decisions can draw on records of what happened and explanations of why particular actions made sense. In chess, these correspond to game histories and natural-language analysis. This paper argues that autonomous agents should use both, bringing together policy learning from interactions and language modeling from written strategic information.

The authors build a large chess dataset containing both game data and language. They use it to present ChessCLIP and ChessGPT as two model examples that integrate the two sources. The contribution therefore includes a shared data resource as well as models: it creates a setting in which action sequences and linguistic analysis can jointly inform learned chess capabilities.

The paper also proposes a comprehensive framework for evaluating a language model's chess ability. Reported experiments support the effectiveness of the models and dataset. The broader significance is a concrete approach to studying how learning from decisions and learning from explanations can be combined, with chess supplying both a decision-making environment and a source of strategic language.
neurips-2023-chessgpt-bridging-policy-le.tldr: ChessGPT combines chess game histories and natural-language analysis through a shared dataset, model examples, and an evaluation framework.

paragraphs: Designing new drug molecules involves two goals: candidates should have desired properties, and the resulting collection should contain varied alternatives. This paper treats molecular diversity as a central part of the generation problem. A method that searches successfully for desirable properties must also explore sufficiently different directions to produce a broad candidate set.

The proposed algorithm, MolRL-MGPT, combines reinforcement learning with multiple GPT agents. The agents are encouraged to collaborate while searching in diverse directions for desirable molecules. This makes coordination among generators part of the design: the system aims to pursue molecular quality and diversity together through the behavior of multiple learning agents.

The authors report promising results on the GuacaMol benchmark and efficacy in designing inhibitors for SARS-CoV-2 protein targets. These findings support the proposed approach as a method for molecular generation and targeted design. The stated contribution is the use of collaborative, diverse searches by multiple GPT agents to address the tension between producing molecules with specific properties and maintaining a varied pool of candidates.
neurips-2023-de-novo-drug-design-using-r.tldr: MolRL-MGPT coordinates multiple GPT agents through reinforcement learning to generate diverse molecules with desired properties.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based inverse-problem solvers reconstruct clean data from corrupted observations, but starting reverse diffusion from noise can make them slow. Recent approaches instead connect clean and corrupted data directly. This paper groups those approaches into a common framework called Direct Diffusion Bridges and shows that their resulting algorithms differ through parameter choices despite their different theoretical motivations.

The authors identify a weakness in that framework: a reconstruction is not necessarily consistent with the observed data. They introduce an inference procedure that explicitly imposes this consistency, producing data Consistent DDB, or CDDB. Because the change operates during inference, it does not require fine-tuning the model to obtain the added constraint.

CDDB improves both perceptual and distortion measures over its counterpart without consistency enforcement, and the authors report state-of-the-art results on both evaluation criteria. Improving both measures means the reported gains move the quality trade-off outward rather than merely exchanging one kind of reconstruction quality for another. The contribution combines a unifying view of existing bridge methods with a practical correction to their reconstruction procedure.
neurips-2023-direct-diffusion-bridge-usi.tldr: CDDB adds data consistency to direct diffusion bridges during inference, improving reported reconstruction quality without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Information design studies how a sender can influence a receiver's actions by choosing what information to reveal. Standard formulations often assume that the receiver reasons in a Bayesian-rational way. This paper considers receivers with other behavioral patterns and asks how information policies can be optimized when those patterns matter.

The proposed framework, HAIDNet, uses neural networks to optimize information design while accommodating multiple representations of human behavior. Simulations show that it can recover policies close to known analytical optima. The authors also apply it to computationally difficult situations involving multiple receivers and to behavior settings for which general analytical solutions are unavailable.

Human-subject experiments provide a further test beyond simulation. The authors report that HAIDNet can learn human behavior from data and use that information to produce more effective policies for human receivers. The significance is an approach that connects behavioral modeling with policy optimization, allowing the assumed response to information to reflect observed behavior instead of relying exclusively on the standard rationality assumption.
neurips-2023-encoding-human-behavior-in-.tldr: HAIDNet learns and incorporates human behavior to optimize information-revelation policies beyond standard Bayesian-rational receiver assumptions.

paragraphs: Sampling from a distribution known only up to a normalization factor is a common scientific computing problem. Markov Chain Monte Carlo can produce asymptotically unbiased samples, but generating a batch may require many iterations, especially in high dimensions. This paper develops a neural sampler that generates samples through a direct transformation instead.

The sampler maps easily generated latent vectors into samples intended to follow the target distribution. Once trained, it can produce large batches without an iterative sampling procedure. The authors introduce two training approaches: one minimizes Kullback-Leibler divergence, and the other minimizes Fisher divergence between the generated and target distributions. These provide two ways to train the same kind of implicit sampling model.

Evaluations cover two-dimensional targets, Bayesian inference, and high-dimensional energy-based models. In the energy-based-model experiment, the sampler produces samples comparable to those from MCMC-based methods while being more than 100 times more efficient. This reported result supports the computational promise of direct neural sampling, with the stated speed advantage tied specifically to that experiment.
neurips-2023-entropy-based-training-meth.tldr: Two divergence-based training methods enable neural samplers to generate batches directly, with substantial efficiency gains in the reported high-dimensional experiment.

paragraphs: Understanding why a model made a prediction is different from understanding why it is uncertain. This paper focuses on the second question. It adapts Shapley values, a framework for assigning contributions among inputs, to quantify how individual features contribute to the conditional entropy of a particular model output.

The authors modify the functions that define the underlying Shapley games so they can explain different kinds of predictive uncertainty. They establish connections between the resulting feature contributions, information-theoretic quantities, and conditional independence testing. These connections give the explanations a statistical interpretation: they relate attributed uncertainty to how information is shared or remains unresolved when other features are considered.

The paper outlines inference procedures with provable finite-sample error-rate control and implements efficient algorithms that perform well on real and simulated data. Potential applications include detecting changes in input distributions, choosing examples for active learning, selecting features, and deciding which feature values to acquire. Across these uses, the shared purpose is to identify which inputs matter for uncertainty in an individual prediction.
neurips-2023-explaining-predictive-uncer.tldr: Information-theoretic Shapley values attribute predictive uncertainty to individual features, supported by statistical connections and finite-sample inference guarantees.

paragraphs: Few-shot generation asks a model to adapt to a new generation task using only a small number of examples. Prior knowledge from earlier datasets can help, but this paper focuses specifically on how that knowledge is stored and recalled. It draws inspiration from human memory mechanisms used during creative activities.

The authors introduce a variational structured memory module that stores both episodic and semantic memories. The module is designed to help existing generative models recall these memories while producing samples. A separate memory-updating strategy handles conversion between the two memory forms and models uncertainty in that conversion, making the changing memory representation an explicit part of the approach.

The memory module is combined with several generative models within a Bayesian framework. Evaluations on few-shot generation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of these memory-augmented models. The contribution is therefore a reusable memory mechanism for generative modeling: it organizes prior experience, supports recall during generation, and accounts for uncertainty as stored memories change, all in service of adapting from limited new data.
neurips-2023-few-shot-generation-via-rec.tldr: A variational memory module helps generative models adapt from few examples by storing, updating, and recalling episodic and semantic memories.

paragraphs: Actor-critic learning couples a policy-improving actor with a critic that evaluates behavior. Analyzing them is difficult when both update on a single timescale, because errors in either component affect the other. Earlier analyses simplified this interaction through independent sampling or tabular representations, leaving the more practical online setting less understood.

This paper studies continuous state spaces with a linearly approximated critic and one Markovian sample per actor update. Such samples follow the ongoing process rather than being independently drawn. The authors develop a framework that tracks and controls error propagation between actor and critic, allowing them to establish convergence in this coupled setting under standard assumptions.

The result guarantees reaching an epsilon-approximate stationary point with sample complexity of order epsilon to the minus two, up to logarithmic factors. Under independent, identically distributed sampling, the logarithmic qualification is removed. The guarantee concerns approximate stationarity rather than global optimality. Beyond this result, the authors identify their error-control framework as a promising approach for analyzing other single-timescale reinforcement learning algorithms.
neurips-2023-finite-time-analysis-of-sin.tldr: The paper proves a finite-sample convergence guarantee for online single-timescale actor-critic with continuous states and a linear critic under standard assumptions.

paragraphs: Representing distances with a tree is useful when data may have a hierarchical structure. This paper asks how the quality of the best tree representation relates to measurements of how tree-like the original distances are. It studies that relationship through hyperbolicity and ultrametricity values collected over triples of points.

The authors compare different norms of these vectors with different norms of tree-fitting error. This puts worst-case and average-style measures into a common formulation: Gromov's classical result corresponds to infinity norms, while normalized one-norms describe average hyperbolicity or ultrametricity. Their HCCRootedTreeFit algorithm has a tight analytical bound connecting its one-norm embedding error to the one-norm of the hyperbolicity vector.

The algorithm exhibits substantially different theoretical and empirical behavior from Gromov's result and related methods. Applying tree-fitting algorithms also reveals that commonly used hierarchical and geometric graph-learning datasets have very different tree fits from synthetic, genuinely tree-like data. The authors interpret this finding as a reason to examine those standard datasets more carefully when using them to study hierarchy.
neurips-2023-fitting-trees-to-ell-1-hype.tldr: The paper links average hyperbolicity to tree-fitting error with a tight bound and questions how tree-like standard hierarchical datasets are.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference estimates model parameters by comparing observed data with simulated information when likelihood calculations are intractable. If the simulator is misspecified, those comparisons can lead to misleading conclusions. This paper focuses on the statistics used for comparison, because their choice affects how strongly the mismatch between the simulator and observations appears in inference.

The proposed approach learns statistics with a regularized loss that penalizes statistics contributing to greater data-model mismatch. This makes robustness part of the representation-learning objective. The method is intended to work across different classes of simulation-based inference, and the authors demonstrate it using neural posterior estimation and approximate Bayesian computation as two distinct use cases.

Experiments involve high-dimensional time-series models with deliberately introduced misspecification, along with real radio-propagation data whose model is known to be misspecified. The authors report superior performance on the artificial cases and robust inference across the studied misspecified settings. They also find that accuracy is maintained when the model is well specified, supporting the value of learning statistics that are less sensitive to model mismatch.
neurips-2023-learning-robust-statistics-.tldr: Learning statistics with a mismatch penalty improves empirical robustness of simulation-based inference when the simulator does not accurately represent the data.

paragraphs: WineSensed brings together wine-label images, written reviews, and human flavor judgments to study relationships between appearance, language, and taste. The dataset contains 897,000 label images and 824,000 reviews from Vivino, covering more than 350,000 unique vintages. Its annotations include year, region, rating, alcohol percentage, price, and grape composition.

To add direct information about perceived flavor, the researchers conduct a tasting experiment with 256 participants. Participants rank wines according to flavor similarity, yielding more than 5,000 pairwise flavor distances for a subset of the dataset. These judgments provide a way to connect the larger collection of visual and textual information with measured human perceptions.

The paper also proposes a low-dimensional concept embedding that combines human experience with automatically computed similarity kernels. The shared representation improves on separate embedding spaces for the reported coarse classification tasks involving wine attributes and for representing perceived flavor. The contribution pairs a multimodal resource with a method for bringing machine-derived similarities and human sensory judgments into one representation.
neurips-2023-learning-to-taste-a-multimo.tldr: WineSensed combines wine images, reviews, and tasting judgments, with a shared embedding that improves reported attribute classification and flavor-perception representation.

paragraphs: Video semantic segmentation assigns a category to every pixel across a sequence. Processing each frame with a powerful image model can repeat expensive work on closely related content. MPVSS reduces that repetition by generating detailed predictions on sparse key frames and carrying those predictions forward to other frames.

A query-based image segmentor first produces binary masks and class predictions on key frames. A flow module then uses the learned queries to estimate a separate, segment-aware flow map for each mask. Warping these mask-flow pairs produces predictions for non-key frames, allowing the system to reuse segmentation work while accounting for how individual segments move.

Experiments on VSPW and Cityscapes show strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. On VSPW, the best Swin-L model exceeds MRCFA with MiT-B5 by a reported 4.0% mIoU while using 26% of its FLOPs. On Cityscapes validation, MPVSS reduces FLOPs by up to fourfold relative to per-frame Mask2Former, with up to 2% mIoU degradation. These comparisons demonstrate the potential of selective segmentation followed by mask propagation.
neurips-2023-mask-propagation-for-effici.tldr: MPVSS propagates segment-specific masks from key frames to reduce video segmentation computation while retaining strong reported accuracy.

paragraphs: A regression method's uncertainty estimates need scrutiny as well as its predictions. This paper studies credible sets at individual input points for a sparse variational Gaussian process method. The central question is whether those sets have appropriate frequentist coverage: how reliably they include the true value across repeated datasets.

The analysis considers eigenvector inducing variables and a rescaled Brownian motion prior. Within that setting, the authors derive guarantees and limitations for both the size and coverage of pointwise credible sets. When sufficiently many inducing variables are used, they precisely characterize asymptotic coverage, identifying circumstances in which the sets are conservative and circumstances in which they are overconfident or misleading.

This distinguishes uncertainty expressed by the variational model from the coverage that uncertainty actually achieves under repeated sampling. The paper illustrates the theoretical findings numerically and discusses connections to other common Gaussian process priors. Its contribution is a detailed account of when pointwise uncertainty is trustworthy for the specified prior and approximation, with the precise asymptotic characterization conditioned on having enough inducing variables.
neurips-2023-pointwise-uncertainty-quant.tldr: The paper characterizes when pointwise credible sets from a sparse variational Gaussian process with a Brownian motion prior are conservative or overconfident.

paragraphs: Hyperparameters can strongly affect a deep learning pipeline's performance, but automatically searching for good settings can be expensive. Researchers therefore often rely on manual experiments informed by experience, domain knowledge, and inexpensive preliminary runs. This paper aims to bring those practical sources of guidance into an automated optimization method.

PriorBand is designed to use both expert beliefs and cheap proxy tasks. Expert beliefs supply information about which settings may be promising, while proxy tasks provide lower-cost evidence during the search. Their joint inclusion addresses the gap identified by the authors between conventional hyperparameter optimization methods and the way researchers manage costly deep learning experiments.

Across a range of deep learning benchmarks, the authors report efficient optimization, improvements when expert guidance is informative, and robustness when that guidance is poor. These are complementary requirements: a useful method should benefit from relevant knowledge without becoming overly dependent on its correctness. The reported results support PriorBand as an empirical approach to incorporating human judgment and inexpensive experimentation into hyperparameter search.
neurips-2023-priorband-practical-hyperpa.tldr: PriorBand combines expert beliefs and cheap proxy tasks for efficient hyperparameter search, with reported gains from good guidance and robustness to poor guidance.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning an unknown probability distribution from a mixture of public and private samples. In its basic setup, both sample sets come from the same distribution, but pure differential privacy protects only the private samples. The question is which distribution classes can be learned under this arrangement and how much data they require.

The authors connect this public-private learning problem to sample compression and an intermediate concept called list learning. These connections approximately recover earlier results for Gaussian distributions and produce new sample-complexity upper bounds for arbitrary mixtures of Gaussians. They also yield results for agnostic and distribution-shift-resistant learners, plus rules showing how learnability behaves when distributions are combined into mixtures or products.

The connection to list learning also gives a lower bound: learning Gaussians in d dimensions privately requires at least d public samples. This is close to the known upper bound of d plus one. Together, the results explain how public information can support private distribution learning and tightly constrain the public sample requirement in the Gaussian case.
neurips-2023-private-distribution-learni.tldr: Connections to compression and list learning yield new public-private distribution-learning bounds, including a nearly tight public-sample requirement for Gaussians.

paragraphs: Inverse optimal control works backward from behavior to characterize the factors governing sequential decisions. This becomes difficult when an agent sees the world imperfectly, the system is nonlinear and stochastic, and the actions themselves are unobserved. The paper develops a probabilistic approach that handles this combination while connecting earlier inverse-control approaches with maximum causal entropy formulations.

The method explicitly models noise in the agent's sensory and motor systems. Together with local linearization, this produces an approximate likelihood for the model parameters that can be computed in one forward pass. The approximation provides a way to evaluate explanations of behavior while accounting for both uncertain perception and noisy action generation.

Evaluations cover stochastic, partially observable versions of two classic control tasks and two human behavioral tasks. The authors show that the method can separate perceptual factors from behavioral costs even when actions simultaneously gather information and pursue practical goals. This matters for interpreting active sensing and learning, where the same behavior may reflect both what an agent knows and what it seeks to achieve.
neurips-2023-probabilistic-inverse-optim.tldr: A probabilistic inverse-control method separates perceptual uncertainty from behavioral costs in nonlinear, partially observable systems with unobserved actions.

paragraphs: This paper describes the entire gradient-flow training trajectory of two-layer diagonal linear networks for regression in the limit of vanishing initialization. Rather than studying only the final fitted solution, it characterizes how learning progresses through intermediate states. The limiting trajectory moves successively between saddle points of the training loss before reaching a minimum one-norm solution.

A recursive algorithm specifies which saddles are visited and when the transitions occur. It resembles LARS, an algorithm used to compute the Lasso path. Starting from zero, coordinates become active over the course of learning, revealing an incremental structure. The proof changes the time parameter using arc length so that transitions between the jumps can be tracked.

The analysis makes negligible assumptions on the data and covers both underparameterized and overparameterized settings. It also includes cases where the number of active coordinates does not increase monotonically, so incremental learning need not mean a steadily growing active set. Numerical experiments support the findings, which describe the training path under the stated network structure and initialization limit.
neurips-2023-saddle-to-saddle-dynamics-i.tldr: For diagonal linear regression networks with vanishing initialization, gradient flow follows a characterized sequence of saddles toward a minimum one-norm solution.

paragraphs: Model merging aims to combine separately fine-tuned models into a multitask model without further training. Simply combining parameters can lose useful information when the models interfere with one another. This paper identifies two sources of that interference: redundant parameter values and disagreement about the signs of corresponding parameter values across models.

TIES-Merging addresses these issues in three stages. It first resets parameters that changed only slightly during fine-tuning, then resolves sign disagreements, and finally merges only values aligned with the selected sign. This makes the direction of parameter changes central to the merging decision rather than treating all contributions as equally compatible.

The authors report improvements over existing merging methods across varied modalities, domains, task counts, model sizes, architectures, and fine-tuning settings. Further analysis examines different interference types and emphasizes the importance of signs. Estimating signs using validation data could improve results further. The findings support the idea that preserving useful task-specific changes requires deciding which contributions can be combined coherently, not merely accumulating parameters from more models.
neurips-2023-ties-merging-resolving-inte.tldr: TIES-Merging reduces interference by trimming small changes, resolving sign conflicts, and combining aligned parameters without additional training.

paragraphs: Learned image compression needs a probability model for the latent features it encodes. Hyperprior-based models often represent those features using a product of individual Gaussian distributions, although actual image latents remain spatially dependent. Autoregressive context models address that mismatch, but their sequential computation adds substantial complexity.

This paper instead introduces a training loss that encourages spatially decorrelated latents, making them better fit the independent probability model. The authors establish the correlation loss as a general plug-in for hyperprior-based compression methods. Because the added mechanism is a training loss, its reported performance gain requires no extra computation during inference or decoding.

Combined with Checkerboard-CM, the approach retains 90% of the autoregressive BD-Rate gains while running around 50 times faster than autoregressive methods. With ChARM-CM, it retains 98% of those gains at around 30 times the speed. These reported combinations illustrate the paper's central strategy: improve the compatibility between learned features and the probability model to obtain a favorable compression-performance and computational-cost trade-off.
neurips-2023-towards-efficient-image-com.tldr: A correlation loss makes image latents better fit independent entropy models, preserving much of the reported autoregressive compression gain at far lower computational cost.

paragraphs: VanillaNet investigates how much neural-network capability can be retained with a deliberately simple architecture. The paper responds to the optimization and deployment complexity of elaborate models by avoiding high depth, shortcut connections, and operations such as self-attention. Its design centers on compact, straightforward layers.

The training procedure includes nonlinear activation functions that are pruned after training to restore the original architecture. This makes the treatment of activations part of the route to a simple final network. The authors position the resulting design as useful for resource-constrained deployment, where architectural complexity can make powerful models harder to use efficiently.

Extensive experiments show performance comparable to well-known deep neural networks and vision Transformers. The stated finding is that this simplified design remains competitive in the reported evaluations. Its broader significance is to establish minimal architecture as a productive direction for model design: strong empirical performance can coexist with fewer structural ingredients, motivating further attention to how layers and training procedures contribute to the capability of a compact network.
neurips-2023-vanillanet-the-power-of-min.tldr: VanillaNet achieves reported performance comparable to established deep networks and vision Transformers using a compact architecture without shortcuts or self-attention.
